transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
Microsoft says its services are approaching
normal levels but are not quite there yet.
One day after an Outlook outage left
millions of customers worldwide without e-mail.
Andrew Kautz, Director of Security and Investigations at
Wired says the outage appears to be
unprecedented in duration and in scale.
>> Well, it's really been hugely disruptive.
I mean, countless businesses around the world,
many local governments,
national governments are experiencing issues.
Airlines are having to divert
customers to alternative communication methods.
We've even seen jails in the United States not able
to release people on bail
because their e-mail systems are down.
>> Microsoft says hacking is not suspected,
but an elevated load may have overstretched its servers.
Microsoft 365 apps have around 430 million customers globally.
Jensen Huang may no longer be
Nvidia's CEO but national security questions remain,
including how much those within
the Trump administration knew and when
about Huang's extramarital relationship
with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia's microchips fuel the global AI race
and underpin the US economy.
NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben reports.
>> Lawmakers from both parties say they want
more information from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
Commerce handles imports and exports,
and so some lawmakers have questions about when he knew
Huang was in contact with a suspected Chinese asset,
and whether the US should have
tightened export controls on advanced chips.
On Thursday, South Carolina Republican Senator Tim Scott,
chair of the banking committee,
said he's summoning Huang and Lutnick
to hearings in early December.
Trump was also asked this week about what he knew and when.
He said he didn't recall receiving a memo with
information about Huang's relationship.
Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News.
>> The US servicemen arrested in the UK on
suspicion of espionage was caught in a sting operation.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports.
>> The 41-year-old Army Lieutenant Colonel currently
being held by UK Metropolitan Police has served
nearly 20 years and had deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan.
A US Army counterintelligence command spokesman confirms
to NPR that the suspect was caught in a sting,
where he didn't know he was speaking to British agents.
UK authorities allege he was attempting to
share sensitive information with Russia.
He's currently being held in London and will be
charged early next week and then transferred to
American custody and charged under
the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
In recent weeks, US bases in the UK have been on
high alert for possible attacks linked to the war in Iran.
But British authorities say this case is not related.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
>> Leadership of the Democratic Party is at
stake after historic midterm wins
as Democrats prepare to take over Congress in January.
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland
says Americans called for change and he is it.
He will challenge Senator Chuck Schumer for Majority Leader.
You're listening to NPR News.
Voter turnout in the midterm elections was
historically high as NPR's Domenico Montanaro reports.
>> Turnout in this election was almost a record.
According to the University of Florida election lab,
which tracks turnout, 49.1 percent of eligible voters
cast ballots across the country in this year's midterm elections.
That's just a tick lower than the 50 percent who
showed up to vote in 2018,
which was the highest mark in more than 100 years.
The states that saw the highest turnout were Maine,
Michigan, and Minnesota.
The lowest were Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Tennessee.
The overall turnout in this election represented
a trend during the Trump era of
higher than usual midterm participation.
But it was still 24 percent lower than
the 2024 presidential election.
Domenico Montanaro, NPR News, Washington.
>> Pope Leo's first big mass in Peru.
[MUSIC]
>> Has brought out hundreds of thousands of people today.
Peru is the last leg of his South American trip.
He returns to Rome on Monday.
A NASA robotic probe close to 50 years into
its space trip is about to cross an epic mile marker.
Next week, Voyager 1 will reach one light day from Earth.
The distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours.
That's some 16 billion miles away,
farther than any man-made object has ever gone before.
On Tuesday night, NASA invites the public to
create a symbolic wave of light around the planet.
Voyager 1 was launched in 1977,
expected to last just five years.
The first spacecraft to leave
our solar system is still going strong collecting data.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Microsoft services near normal after Outlook outage left millions without email
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged Chinese spy ties draw congressional scrutiny of Commerce Secretary Lutnick
US Army Lieutenant Colonel arrested in UK on suspicion of espionage in sting operation
Democrats prepare for Congress; Senator Chris Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Majority Leader
Midterm voter turnout near record high at 49.1 percent nationwide
Pope Leo holds large mass in Peru, last leg of South American trip
NASA's Voyager 1 nears one light day from Earth, farthest human-made object
